I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01882

What matters to Shiism is the final Event of our Aeon, our age of the world: the ultimate reign of the Imam, who will restore all things to their rightful place and their truth—a universal restoration (apokatastasis)—and who for this reason is called the Qâ'im, the Resurrector. Shiite theologians agree, however, that the Imam never ruled out appearing “privately” to help a follower suffering material or moral distress: a lost traveler, for example, or a believer overcome by despair.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01883

Although Shiite sacred history abounds in such visions of divine manifestation, they occur only at the Imam's initiative. Almost always he appears as an extraordinarily beautiful young man; and almost always, with rare exceptions—we shall encounter one below—the person granted the vision realizes only afterward whom he has seen. A strict anonymity ordinarily surrounds these appearances: the very anonymity that protects religious experience from being turned into a social institution.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01884

“Many men,” writes one of our theologians, 'Alî Asghar Borûjardî, “have seen the perfect beauty of this Chosen One [the Twelfth Imam], but they recognized him only later, after he had left them.” They understand because the help they received, whether material or spiritual, could only have come from the Imam. Some have seen him during the pilgrimage to Mecca; others in the mosque of Kufa, the ancient Shiite city par excellence; still others in one or another Shiite holy place.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01885

But the experience is never a collective vision. Even when people “see” him, they are incapable of recognizing him. That is exactly what the Great Occultation means. The Imam comes and goes everywhere in the world without being present as a part of any one place, without being fixed or contained within it.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01886

The same anonymity surrounds his companions, a word that has both a broad and a narrower meaning. In the broad sense, it refers to the esoteric hierarchy we have discussed several times, whose membership is determined by symbolic correspondences. Its members remain unknown among us, generation after generation; whenever one departs, a companion from the next lower rank is raised to take his place. We have seen this same idea in Sufism. In the narrower sense, the companions of the Hidden Imam are an elite within the elite, young men or “knights” (javânmardân) who serve him constantly in his immediate company.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01887
We shall encounter them in the account of the “Journey to the Green Island” translated below.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01888

Yet both groups are hidden under the same veil of anonymity: the first for the reasons already given (Book VI, pp. 278 ff.), and the second because even the few chosen people who have met them “in the land of the Hidden Imam” cannot recognize them any more readily than they could recognize the Imam himself. As the theologian just cited writes: “No one knows them, and they make themselves known to no one. Just as men cannot recognize the Imam, they never recognize a single one of his companions or pages. These companions do not frequent men's houses. Their activities and occupations are unknown.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01889

“Sometimes they come into contact with human beings, but no one knows their true state or condition. In deserts, on islands of the Ocean, in the heart of mountains or the depths of valleys, they sometimes pitch their tents. And so many travelers, caravaneers, and wanderers who have lost their way have seen tents, dwellings, castles, and enchanting green places rise before them in the middle of arid deserts... Some have been allowed to enter. They saw and understood. They returned, but could never again find the way back, or show anyone else how to get there.”
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01890

Because both groups remain hidden in the same way, there is in fact no definitive criterion by which to distinguish their members. Nor would it serve any purpose to try. Since the Imam's “place” is everywhere, we can say of all of them that their own “place” is near him. Together they form that elite, that “knighthood,” through which the higher world communicates with the lower—and without which humanity could not continue to exist. Through them runs a continual selection of beings who transcend ordinary humanity, from Adamic humanity (the three hundred who bear the likeness of Adam) to seraphic humanity, embodied in the Supreme Pole (the one who bears the likeness of Seraphiel).
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01891

Every devout Shiite longs to be counted among them, or raised from the dead in their company, at the Imam's side in the final battle (see the pilgrim's prayer translated here, pp. 458 ff.). In developing this theme, Shiite theosophy has given vivid expression to something that both distinguishes it and reveals its deep kinship with other spiritual traditions. Later we shall try to make these resonances felt by developing the theme of “spiritual knighthood.”
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01892

The anonymity required of the mystical knighthood surrounding the Hidden Imam, in either sense, is as strict, as we noted earlier, as that of the knights of the Grail: one cannot reach them unless they themselves lead one to them. Suhrawardî's work gave us the opportunity (in Book II) to trace the signs that lead from Iran's heroic epic to its mystical epic, along a tradition parallel to the adventures of Parsifal and pointing likewise toward the realm of the Grail.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01893

Later we shall show how Shiite literature about the Hidden Imam guides us along a converging path. The same ethical rule governs both the anonymity of the mystical knighthood that forms the esoteric hierarchy and the kettnân, the discipline of keeping sacred secrets imposed by the Imams. It is observed by every believer who has been tested (momtahan), that is, initiated into the spiritual meaning of Imamism.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01894

Since 'Alî al-Samarrî's final words—“From now on, the matter belongs to God alone”—this spiritual attitude, this ethos, has been marked by desperatio fiducialis: a despair that nevertheless trusts, an unshakably confident pessimism sustained by the coming dawn of the Imam's appearance. Through it, every follower who has “proved himself” answers and corresponds to the watchfulness of the Unseen Ones. This is how the dawn draws near; this is what it means to “be a companion of the Imam.”
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01895
We can understand all the more clearly why anyone who publicly claimed to be a “companion of the Imam” and presumed to speak in his name would be committing a betrayal, and could only be an impostor.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01896

We shall not try to pierce that veil of anonymity here. Instead, we shall translate a few accounts from witnesses who “were led there and saw.” Even if they cannot guide us back along the path they took, they can at least tell us what they saw when they left the outer world and entered, “between times,” what we can only call by the name Suhrawardî himself coined in Persian: Nâ-kojâ-âbâd, the “Land of No-Where.” It is an inner place, genuinely a land (âbâd), yet one cannot say where it is, because no direction toward it can be found by using the cardinal points of the sensory world. It is the land of “theophanic visions,” and belongs to what Suhrawardî also called the “eighth clime.” The universe of the Malakût, the spiritual realm parallel to the sensory universe, has its own space and its own arrangement of places.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01897

We can begin to imagine how that space relates to the space of our world only when we understand, with our philosophers, how a spiritual substance “envelops” a material one—how the soul is the body's “spiritual place.”
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01898

Among the many accounts of the Imam's appearances “during the Great Occultation,” the four texts translated below belong to different types. Two of them—the first, concerning the founding of Jam-Karân, and the fourth, concerning an encounter in the desert—bring the believer directly into the presence of the Imam himself. The other two—the journey to the Green Island and the journey to the five islands—bring the believer into the presence of the Imam's companions or sons. In every case the meeting follows a secret decision by the Imam. A person must become capable of receiving such a meeting; but no one can decide to meet the Imam, still less bring the meeting about by force of will.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01899

An anecdote below will remind us of this. Sometimes the Imam's presence breaks into the very place where a believer or pilgrim is standing, and there transports that person into his presence (the fourth account). Sometimes the visionary experience begins when figures “belonging to the Imam's world” appear and gradually lead the pilgrim into that world (the first and second accounts). At other times it begins with an initiatory prelude—such as a sea voyage—that, without the travelers' knowledge, carries them into an unknown world (the third account).
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01900

All these accounts share one remarkable feature: the passage from the geography of the sensory world to that of the unknown world occurs without the travelers being aware of the precise moment of transition. They recognize it only when they are already “somewhere else.”
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01901

Another striking detail is that the Imam's world may break into ours and leave a material trace behind, such as a building erected at his command. More unsettling still, the pilgrim may bring back an object as evidence of the encounter: a book or a purse, for example. Sometimes the event makes the account into a genuine narrative of initiation—initiation into Shiite teaching, into the mystery of the Imamate (the second and third accounts).
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01902

Yet there is something, as the account of the journey to the Green Island warns us, that we shall never know, because the discipline of sacred secrecy forbids—or at that time forbade—it to be put in writing. These accounts suggest that the spiritual place outside ordinary space is present everywhere: what we might call the ubiquity of Nâ-kojâ-âbâd. In relation to the bounded, enclosing space of the sensory world, the spiritual place is nowhere precisely because it is equally everywhere (see below, II, 4).
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01903

Finally, these accounts, together with the many others like them, must be read as a continuation of the sacred biography of the Twelfth Imam. When we say that the Twelfth Imam has, for ten centuries, been the history of Shiite consciousness, we are speaking neither metaphorically nor by some trick of naming things. We mean it in the thoroughly “realist” sense of the mundus imaginalis.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01904

The point in our world where the Imam's place becomes visible is the mazhar: the theater and mirror in which his place appears. It is therefore not within that mirror that we should afterward look for the Imam himself. Suhrawardî explains this admirably, in complete agreement with what Swedenborg would later teach concerning the world of visions. In the mystical study of mirrors, the faculty that perceives appearances in them is the imagination itself—a katoptron, a mirror, and specifically the mirror of consciousness.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01905

To call these visions, these manifestations, the biography and history of the Twelfth Imam is therefore to say that this history takes place in the parallel world. Compared with history as the word is ordinarily understood, it is an anti-history. It does not enter ordinary history any more than a reflected image enters into the substance of a mirror, as black pigment, for example, enters into black wood.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01906

The place in which it unfolds is spiritual, just as its time lies “between times.” These manifestations free the human being from the laws of history and from the space in which ordinary history occurs. They are not subject to the laws of historical causation; the Hidden Imam's secret history cannot be “explained” by the workings of those laws. The principle underlying these manifestations is a principle of release from historical causation. It moves against the current of our religious theologies and philosophies that “seek God in history.” The Twelfth Imam's “history” is an escape from History. Unless we understand this, we cannot enter the Imam's world.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01907
We will fall back upon “scientific” explanations whose clearest result may be to abolish the very reality they set out to explain.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-01908
Chapter II In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
en-book-7-ch-2-s1
1. The Sanctuary of Jam-Karân
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-01909

The accounts translated here will confirm that, although the Hidden Imam's return dominates the whole of Shiite consciousness, the Shiite community's relationship with its Imam necessarily remains within the dimensio mystica, the mystical dimension.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-01910

Indeed, it would be hard to find a book about the Imam that did not devote a chapter to testimonies from people who have seen him, whether in dreams or while awake. These accounts together constitute the “history”—more precisely, the sacred history—of the Twelfth Imam during the Great Occultation, a time “between times.” We have therefore said that this history itself unfolds “between times.” The duration of an experience of this kind has its own measure: it cannot be fitted into the sequence of chronological time or measured in its units.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-01911

We can establish the visionary's place in ordinary chronology before and after the experience. But compared with the event itself, all we possess then is the chrysalis, the empty shell: for during the event, the visionary was not there, in ordinary time and space.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-01912

Many anecdotes illustrate that such an event depends neither on human initiative nor on a person's decision. Their origins may be difficult to trace, yet they remain eloquent because they say exactly what they need to say. I shall recount one particularly characteristic story, as an Iranian friend told it to me some years ago. A mojtahed—one of those scholars who devote their whole lives to studying and interpreting the Shiite traditions—longed passionately to see the Hidden Imam. To this end he performed every kind of pious act.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-01913

Then one night he dreamed of a figure who told him that he would see the Imam at dawn on a particular morning, at the workshop of a particular craftsman near one of the gates of Isfahan. He hesitated, but the same dream came to him on three successive nights. So he went to the place indicated. Just as he was about to enter the craftsman's house, a young man came out. The scholar went inside, introduced himself, and carefully explained at length why he had come so early.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-01914

“But the Imam was here only a moment ago,” the craftsman replied, “just as you were coming in.” My Iranian friend explained the story this way: the Imam can take on any outward appearance. It is not for you to seek a vision of him. It is for him to decide whether you have the capacity to see him—whether you truly are one of his companions, whether you belong to his world. To belong to the world of the Imam's companions is to have the capacity to perceive spiritual Forms, to “see things in Hûrqalyâ.” Neither human effort nor human learning can create or activate this capacity. An ordinary person may be granted it just as readily as a shaykh, a great spiritual master, or a learned scholar. The initiative belongs to the Imam.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-01915

That is how Shiite consciousness understands it, and the origin of the sanctuary of Jam-Karân offers a striking illustration. The sanctuary of Samarra in Iraq marks the place where the Imam became hidden from human sight, from the eyes of the flesh. The sanctuary of Jam-Karân in Iran is one of the places where he appears to a different, subtle faculty of vision.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-01916

Without recognizing this faculty, any account of what a human being is remains incomplete. It will either treat concrete spiritual reality as though it were material, or reduce it to fantasy, hallucination, or a mere idea. That is why we have already connected the study of visionary consciousness with Suhrawardî's account of reality. More than any other, his philosophy established a place in the order of being for the “world of visions,” and his influence in this respect has endured over the centuries.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-01917
Thus a pilgrimage to Samarra or Jam-Karân, whether made physically or inwardly, presupposes for every pilgrim a passage beyond sensory perception into a higher mode of perceiving.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-01918

Jam-Karân is an oasis about a league and a half southeast of the city of Qomm, in the desert, near mountains that at dusk take on shapes as fantastic as the fragile mud-brick buildings of the little settlement. There, in the fourth/tenth century, following an appearance of the Twelfth Imam to a shaykh who lived in the village, a sanctuary was built that became a place of pilgrimage for all Twelver Shiites. We are especially concerned with the circumstances of that appearance.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-01919

Our information about the founding of the mosque at Jam-Karân by order of the Twelfth Imam goes back to one of Ibn Bâbûyeh's many works. That book has been lost, but fortunately the account was preserved in a History of Qomm written by one of his contemporaries. We found it in one of the learned compilations assembled by the eminent Iranian Shiite scholar of the preceding century, Mîrzâ Hosayn Nûrî.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-01920

The account is told in the first person, in the words of the shaykh who, one night in Ramadan 373/February 984, was granted the privilege of speaking with the Twelfth Imam. This date—an entirely external marker, of course—is only about forty years later than the date assigned to the beginning of the Great Occultation. The opening of the story contains details particularly worth noting because they recall symbolic practices familiar from rites of initiation.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-01921

First comes the changing of clothes. We find the same feature in other accounts that likewise resemble initiation narratives. In the “Story of the White Cloud” (above, Book V, Chapter III, 3), for example, we saw the Imam appear at one point wearing two robes whose symbolic colors announced that the participants had crossed into the Malakût, the spiritual world. There, too, an episode included by Qâzî Sa'îd Qommî in his interpretation showed the Fifth Imam, Mohammad Bâqir, entering an oratory to change his robe before leading his disciple into the Malakût, then putting his original robe back on upon returning.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-01922

The successive putting on of robes corresponding to the stages of mystical ascent is also a well-known feature of the rites of the Mithraic mysteries. Putting off one garment and putting on another is, in fact, a ritual that necessarily accompanies passage from one world to another. It signifies that one cannot enter a higher world with the nature and faculties one possesses in a lower world.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-01923

As we shall see from the opening of the story, the gestures made by the shaykh of Jam-Karân, confused and alarmed by the extraordinary summons he has received, correspond point for point to familiar rites of initiation. Although there is no formal liturgical ceremony, the meaning is the same. Twice the shaykh tries to put on his ordinary clothes, and twice an insistent voice warns him that he is mistaken. Those clothes are not his. They belong to his outward, everyday life, not to his soul. Only the soul's garments can be worn for a temporary entrance into the Malakût, because they alone truly belong to him.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-01924

The everyday garment is neither genuine nor his own; the sacred garment belongs to the soul, like the garment worn by the initiate at the moment of initiation. Here, too, when the shaykh is warned of his error, he finds the garment that is truly his and that alone allows him to appear at the place to which he has been summoned. Precisely because it is his own garment, he now finds it spontaneously, without having to search.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-01925

Another detail: the shaykh searches in vain for the key to his house so that he can leave. The same voice tells him that no key is needed to go out and enter the world where he is expected. Nor does the exile in Suhrawardî's initiation narratives need a key to leave his prison and set out to meet the Angel; others have already opened the door for him.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-01926

Finally, when his mysterious visitors bring the shaykh into the Imam's presence, he sees him surrounded by dignified figures whose clothing reveals them to be among the Imam's companions. Close to the Imam sits a venerable sage reading aloud. The visionary recognizes Khezr (Khadîr), the mysterious prophet always encountered near the Spring of Life, the initiator of all who have had no human master—or no master other than the Imam. He has appeared often and will appear again in the texts presented here.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-01927

A companion of the Twelfth Imam, he is even identified by some with the Imam himself. Every detail thus seems to be in its proper place, showing us that the Imam's presence takes a person out of the world of ordinary perception and suggesting where the visionary is brought, where the meeting with the Imam takes place. Let us now follow the text.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-01928

“The shaykh 'Afîf Sâlih Jam-Karânî (called simply Hasan later in the account) related the following: On the night of Tuesday, the seventeenth of Ramadan in the year 373 of the Hijra (22 February 984), I was sleeping in my house when several men knocked at the door. It was past midnight. They woke me, calling, ‘Get up, and answer the summons of Imam Mohammad al-Mahdî, Sâhib al-Zamân, the Lord of the Age, who is calling you.’ I got up, somewhat anxious, and began to prepare myself. ‘They will surely have left before I am ready,’ I thought. I put on my shirt.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-01929

“But a voice said, ‘Take off that shirt; it is not yours.’ In my confusion I tried to put on my sarâwîl, my breeches. Again the same voice said, ‘Those do not belong to you. Take the breeches that are yours.’ So I put aside the garment, took my own, and put it on. Then I began looking for the key to my door so that I could go out. Again I heard the voice: ‘The door is open!’ When I reached it and found that it was indeed open, I saw a group of noble-looking men standing there. I greeted them; they returned my greeting and said, ‘Welcome!’ Then they led me to the place where the mosque now stands.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-01930

“As I looked around, I saw a throne (takht) with splendid cushions arranged upon it. A young man of about thirty was reclining against four of them. Before him sat a pîr—a shaykh, a wise elder—holding a book and reading aloud to the young man. More than sixty people were gathered around the throne, engaged in prayer. Some wore white robes, others green. The pîr whom I saw reading was His Holiness Khezr (Khadir). Then he made a sign to me.”
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-01931

We have reached the moment when we learn why the Imam summoned the shaykh. A man named Hasan Moslem has seized and desecrated this holy ground. The shaykh Hasan Jam-Karânî is to carry a message to the usurper: he must return the land, and a house of worship must be built upon it.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-01932
“At that moment the Imam called me by name and said, ‘Go to Hasan Moslem and tell him this: “For five years you have cultivated this land, and this year you have harvested its crop once again.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-01933

“But from now on you are no longer permitted to cultivate it. You must give back all the profit you have drawn from it, so that a mosque may be built on this very spot.” Say this to Hasan Moslem as well: “This is holy ground, chosen by God from among other lands.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-01934

“But you have taken possession of it as though it belonged to you. God has already taken two young sons from you, yet your conscience has not awakened. If you do not obey this command, other misfortunes will befall you until your conscience awakens.”’”
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-01935

Shaykh Hasan Jam-Karânî then said to the Imam, “My lord and protector, I need a sign for this mission. Without some sign and proof, people will not listen to my words or believe what I tell them.” The Imam replied, “We shall give you a sign here, so that your words will be believed. Go now and carry our message.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-01936

“First seek out Sayyed Abû'l-Hasan Rezâ. Tell him to rise and go to Hasan Moslem. Let him demand an account of the profits that man has taken from the land over so many years, recover them from him, and use them to build the mosque. Let him summon the leading men of the region from Rahaq to Ardahâl, which is our domain, and see the building of the sanctuary through to completion.”
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-01937

The Imam then sets out the conditions of the waqf, the charitable religious endowment, and prescribes the ritual rules pilgrims must follow when they pray at his sanctuary: the order of invocations and readings, and the number of rak'at, the prescribed cycles of prayer marked by bowing and prostration. These are the rules that pilgrims to Jam-Karân have observed for ten centuries. “For the pilgrim,” the Imam says, “who performs this prayer of two rak'at in the prescribed way, it will be as though he had performed it in the Ancient Sanctuary at Mecca”—that is, within the Kaaba itself. At a sign from the Imam, Shaykh Hasan Jam-Karânî takes his leave.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-01938

But twice, after he has walked a few steps, the Imam calls him back. The first time, the Imam tells him that in the flock of a shepherd named Ja'far Kâshânî he will find a particular male goat, with a thick black-and-white coat marked by seven distinctive signs. He must buy this animal, offer it in sacrifice, and distribute its meat among the sick and disabled, who will then be healed. This sacrifice corresponds to the sacrifice of the cow described in the second sura of the Quran (2:63–69), an act of atonement and purification.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-01939

Those Quranic verses clearly recall the Book of Numbers (19:1–10). The Imam calls the shaykh back a second time to announce that his “presence” will remain in this place for seven days: until the night in Ramadan known as the “Night of Destiny”.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-01940

Clearly, the Imam's words are rich in symbols. Shaykh Hasan Jam-Karânî continues his account. He leaves the place and time of divine manifestation, where he alone had been privileged to witness what occurred, and returns to the continuous flow of ordinary time and the space of everyday perception. The fabric of daily events, interrupted by a supernatural intervention it cannot contain, resumes its course. What happens next will establish the only link in time available to us between the visionary event and an event belonging to visible history: the Imam's predictions will be fulfilled, and the mosque will be built.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-01941

“I returned home,” says the shaykh, “and spent the rest of the night in deep meditation, until daybreak.” He then goes to find a friend, and together they make their way to the place where the Imam appeared. To their amazement, they see a collection of chains and nails lying on the ground. Shaykh Hasan recognizes the promised sign. The two friends hurry to visit Sayyed Abû'l-Hasan Rezâ, as the Imam instructed. There the shaykh discovers that he is expected.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-01942

“You are from Jam-Karân, are you not?” the Sayyed asks. The shaykh tells him what happened the previous night. “Hasan,” the Sayyed replies, “last night, while I slept, someone spoke to me in a dream: ‘A man named Hasan will come to you from Jam-Karân in the morning. You must believe his words, trust what he tells you; his words will be our words. Do not reject him.’ I woke up, and I have been waiting for you ever since.”
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-01943

From that moment Sayyed Abû'l-Hasan Rezâ directs the undertaking, following the Imam's instructions as delivered by Shaykh Hasan. Riding together, the three companions first make their way to the shepherd Ja'far Kâshânî beside the track. The goat described by the Imam is indeed there, and runs of its own accord toward Shaykh Hasan. They agree to buy it, but the shepherd Ja'far makes an extraordinary declaration, swearing that it is true: “Until now I had never seen this goat. It had never been part of my flock.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-01944

“I saw it for the first time this morning and tried in vain to catch it. And now it comes running to meet you.” The goat is sacrificed at the appointed place. Hasan Moslem, who had seized the holy land, is summoned and compelled to return what does not belong to him. The notables of Rahaq are called together.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-01945

In short, everything necessary is done for the Imam's mosque. Sayyed Abû'l-Hasan Rezâ takes the mysterious chains and nails to his home in Qomm. Fastened to the gateway of his house, they have extraordinary effects upon those who touch them.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-01946
But after the Sayyed's death, it seems, they disappear as mysteriously as they had appeared on the ground at Jam-Karân when dawn broke at the end of that visionary night.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-01947

Such, in brief, are the events preserved in the tradition of Jam-Karân. There, near the village, within a green enclosure, now stands the sanctuary built according to the Imam's instructions. For almost ten centuries it has been a pilgrimage destination for Shiites, particularly Iranian Shiites. It is still visited by large numbers of pilgrims today, yet remains surrounded by a remarkable discretion, like everything that concerns devotion to the Hidden Imam.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-01948

One glorious late autumn in Iran, in 1962, we had the opportunity to visit Jam-Karân with two dear Iranian companions. We had spent the day in the village of Kahak, in a high valley of the nearby mountains, where Mollâ Sadrâ Shîrâzî had sought refuge for some ten years of solitude. One of my companions was the man whose dream I shall recount at the end of this chapter—a dream that bears witness, if any were needed, to the intensity of the Imam's presence in Shiite hearts. I retain an extraordinary memory of that pilgrimage.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-01949

Perhaps it is because, in a place of such strange geological surroundings, where the Imam's mosque stands upon the earth as a splendid challenge posed to our age by faith in the Unseen Ones, everything seems possible. In that immense, silent landscape, stories such as those we shall tell in this chapter acquire a presence and conviction wholly different from what they have when we read them in our own countries, amid the noise of cities or beside busy highways. In the desert, no track looks more like another than one desert track.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-01950

We had lost our way, and one of my companions loudly called out to a rider who happened, providentially, to pass nearby: “Which way is the sanctuary of the Imâm al-zamân, the Imam of this Age?” Those words, Imâm al-zamân, ringing out into the silence of that vast solitude, as pure as the immense sky above us, suddenly gave the One whom they had named with such hope and devotion for so many centuries the compelling force of something real. It lasted only for a flash, yet it was unmistakably real... for all three of us were seeking the road to him, and someone was showing us the way.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-01951

We said earlier that the story of the foundation of the mosque at Jam-Karân belongs to a particular kind of manifestation of the Imam during the Great Occultation. In accounts of this kind, the person granted the experience is not only brought into the Imam's presence but also knows that it is the Imam before him.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-01952

The Imam's presence suddenly enters the visionary's surroundings and envelops him “as a spiritual substance envelops a material substance.” Other accounts tell of pilgrims who are not brought into the Imam's presence, yet are nonetheless “at the Imam's home.” They must also travel through stages of a mysterious geography that will never be found on our maps, since it belongs to the “eighth clime.” The first two of the three accounts that follow are of this kind.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
en-book-7-ch-2-s2
2. The Journey to the Green Island in the White Sea
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-01953

The first of these three accounts, the journey to the Green Island (al-Jazîrat al-khazrâ), was recorded by Majlisî in his great encyclopedia of Shiite hadith traditions. It comes from a document once kept in the library of the sanctuary at Najaf in Iraq—the sanctuary of the First Imam, 'Alî ibn Abî Tâlib. We have already mentioned this place, for it was in the treasury of the same sanctuary that our friend Osman Yahya discovered Haydar Âmolî's autograph manuscript of the Tafsîr 'irfânî. The document was written in the hand of an eminent shaykh from Kufa: al-Fazl ibn Yahyâ ibn 'Alî al-Tayyibî al-Kûfî.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-01954

This was the man who had heard the account directly from the person who had lived through that extraordinary experience: an Iranian shaykh from Mazandaran, the province along the southern shore of the Caspian Sea, named 'Ali ibn Fazel Mazandarani (and thus a compatriot of our Haydar Amoli; see above, Book IV, Chapter I).
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-01955

The man who wrote the account down, Shaykh al-Fazl ibn Yahya, took great care to describe the circumstances. He himself was at Karbala, in Iraq, making a pilgrimage to the shrine of the Third Imam, Imam Hosayn, the Prophet's grandson, honoured as the “Prince of Martyrs” (Sayyed al-shohada). On the fifteenth of Sha'ban in the year 699 of the Hijra, corresponding to 19 May 1299—a significant date, since the night of the fifteenth of Sha'ban marks the birthday of the Twelfth Imam, the Hidden Imam—he had a long conversation with two distinguished shaykhs who had also come on pilgrimage.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-01956

They were Shaykh Shamsoddin ibn Najih al-Hilli and Shaykh Jalaloddin 'Abdollah ibn al-Hawam al-Hilli, both from the mountains of Hilla in Syria, long a centre of Shiite life. They told our writer of an extraordinary story they had heard shortly before, while making a pilgrimage to Samarra—another Shiite holy place, where, as we recalled above, the Eleventh Imam, Hasan al-'Askari, died and his son entered the Occultation. At Samarra an Iranian shaykh had told them of “the strange and wonderful things he had contemplated and seen with his own eyes on the Green Island in the White Sea.”
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-01957

Naturally, their listener was immediately consumed by the desire to hear the story from its hero's own lips. He set out at once for Samarra, hoping to find him still there. As it happened, he had the good fortune to meet him instead at Hilla. The meeting was made easier because the Iranian shaykh had taken up residence there with a fellow Mazandarani, Sayyed Fakhroddin Hasan Mazandarani, who had settled in Hilla. They were introduced amid all the charming courtesies of Eastern hospitality. It emerged that, in Wasit, the Iranian shaykh had known the father and brother of the man who would now record his story; they were almost family.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-01958

Other shaykhs from Hilla and the surrounding country arrived in their turn. And on the evening of 11 Shawwal 699, or 12 July 1299—almost exactly two months after he had first heard the story indirectly at Najaf—Shaykh al-Fazl ibn Yahya al-Kufi listened, spellbound, as did the rest of his learned audience, all of them Shiites, to the account of Shaykh 'Ali ibn Fazel Mazandarani. He assures us that he wrote down everything faithfully. He may have changed a word here or there, but neither the meaning nor the events were altered.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-01959

'Ali ibn Fazel's own account is equally rich in detail. It begins with a short introduction that tells us, among other things, the kind of man we are dealing with: a learned and devout man, showing no sign of a disposition toward what we today call schizophrenia. He explains that he had spent several years in Syria, specifically in Damascus, studying the disciplines that make up the traditional Islamic sciences. Among other things, he studied Qur'anic sciences under a shaykh from Andalusia, Shaykh Zaynoddin 'Ali al-Maghrebi al-Andalusi, to whom he became especially attached—not only because of the man's learning but because of his extraordinary gentleness.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-01960

For example, whenever this shaykh, who followed the Maliki school of law, had occasion to mention the Shiites, he would say, “The Imami scholars hold such-and-such an opinion on this point,” instead of using insulting names and hurling abuse, as all the other madrasa teachers did.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-01961

Unfortunately, after several years, the distinguished Andalusian shaykh decided to settle in Egypt. The prospect of parting was as painful to the teacher as it was to his pupil, and no less painful to a whole group of other students, expatriates (ghoraba') who had grown attached to him.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-01962

Since travel formalities and expenses in those days did not present the complications familiar to us, especially for a shaykh travelling with his pupils, they made the simplest possible decision: they would all go to Egypt together. (We shall learn at the end of the story that this journey included a memorable episode of which the narrator says nothing for now.) In Cairo, Shaykh Zaynoddin al-Andalusi took up residence at the famous al-Azhar Mosque, where he gave lessons. The most eminent people in Egypt came to visit and consult him.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-01963

In short, everything went splendidly, and the students too lived in the most agreeable circumstances. Then, nine months later, misfortune arrived in the form of a company of travellers from Andalusia. “One of them,” says the narrator, “was carrying a letter from our shaykh's father. His father told him that he had been stricken by a serious illness and wished to see him before he died. He urged him to set out without delay.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-01964

“Our shaykh was deeply moved by his father's letter and wept. He resolved to leave for Andalusia at once. Some of his disciples again decided to accompany him. I was one of them, because the shaykh was very fond of me and because I greatly liked the prospect of travelling in his company.”
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-01965

What route did they take? How far did they travel by caravan? Where did they board a ship? 'Ali ibn Fazel says nothing about any of this. What we do know is that, scarcely had he set foot on Andalusian soil when, at the very first stopping place, he was seized by a violent fever. His shaykh was distressed, but he was still five days' journey from his father's home and had to hurry on. He therefore entrusted the sick man to the care of the local preacher (khatib): once recovered, his pupil would easily be able to rejoin him.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-01966

But events took a very different course. The fever kept 'Ali in bed for three days. At the end of the third day, when it had subsided, he went out for some air in the village streets. There he noticed a group of men who had brought several consignments of goods and “had come from the mountains bordering the shore of the Western Sea (the Atlantic?).” He made inquiries. “They come,” he was told, “from a region near the land of the Berbers, in the direction of the peninsula of the Rawafiz”—that is, the “Dissenters,” a disparaging name used by Sunnis for Shiites.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-01967

The news filled him with joy and gave him a great longing to know that country. He asked for more precise directions. “From here to that country,” he was told, “is a journey of twenty-five days. Of those, two days are spent crossing a desert where there is not a trace of water or cultivation. Beyond it, the villages follow one after another.”
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-01968

'Ali ibn Fazel hired a donkey for three dirhams, joined the group, and set off on his great adventure. He does not tell us whether or how they crossed the Strait of Gibraltar—or at least the man who recorded his account omitted it. In any case, he reached the far side of the great desert safely. There he learned that the “peninsula of the Shiites” was another three days' march away, and he continued alone. Already it is far from certain that we are following a route that could be traced on our geographical maps.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-01969

At last our traveller came to a peninsula surrounded by four walls, each defended by high, massive towers. The outermost wall ran along the seashore. He entered through a monumental gateway called the “Gate of the Berbers,” appropriately enough, since he had come from the direction of Berber country. He was shown the way to the principal mosque, an imposing building on the western side of the city, overlooking the sea. Exhausted, he found a secluded corner of the mosque and rested. Suddenly the voice of the muezzin rose, chanting the call to prayer.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-01970

To understand the exile's emotion, we must recall the secrecy in which Shiites, the faithful of the holy Imams, had so long been forced to live by bitter persecution across vast stretches of the Islamic world. For the first time in his life, 'Ali ibn Fazel heard, ringing out from a mosque's minaret at the end of the ritual call to prayer, the Shiite invocation asking that the “Joy” be hastened. This is the traditional name for the joy of the Imam's coming: the future appearance of the one who reigns invisibly, incognito, over the present age.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-01971

Could he truly have found his own people at last? Tears filled his eyes. He watched groups of worshippers perform their ritual ablutions at a spring flowing beneath a great tree, east of the mosque's outer enclosure; all followed the Shiite rite. Then a handsome man, whose whole bearing expressed dignity and gentleness, stepped away from the groups to lead the prayers. 'Ali saw that everyone performed the service, from beginning to end, according to the practices handed down by the Shiite Imams.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-01972
But he himself was too overcome by the exhaustion of his journey. He stayed in his corner, resting, and did not join in the prayer.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-01973

This was precisely what everyone reproached him for when, the prayers ended, they noticed his presence. First of all, who was he? What was he doing there? 'Ali ibn Fazel could have justified his presence simply by saying that he too was an Iranian Shiite.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-01974

But he said nothing of the kind. A Shiite, especially a Shiite travelling alone, and particularly in those days, would never be the first to speak openly. He confined himself to saying that he was an Iraqi—he had, after all, lived in Iraq—and a Muslim. He recited the twofold profession of faith, affirming the oneness of God (tawhid) and Muhammad's mission as Prophet.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-01975

But the others answered that these two affirmations might make him a Muslim; they were not enough to make him a mu'min, a true believer, faithful in the fullest sense of the word. Why did he not pronounce the third testimony, and so declare himself a true believer? Our traveller, carrying the discipline of secrecy to its very limit, pretended not to know what this third testimony was and asked them to explain.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-01976

The shaykh who had led the prayers then revealed the secret of the Imamate to him: the names of the Twelve Imams, the Twelve Friends of God (Awliya' Allah), the twelve Names that the divine voice had revealed to the Prophet during his Night Journey, when he was carried in ecstasy from heaven to heaven. These were the Names inscribed in blazing letters upon a mysterious emerald tablet in Fatima's possession; the very Names that Adam had contemplated, written in letters of light upon the pillars of the Throne before he left paradise; the Names that Haydar Amoli himself had seen in a vision in the night sky over Baghdad, written in gold and encircled with lapis lazuli.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-01977

In that instant, all the traveller's fear and reserve vanished, together with his fatigue. There followed a moving scene of recognition between brothers: “I am one of you; I too am a Shiite.” Now everyone vied to care for him and show him kindness, consideration and respect. As was customary, they found him a little space in an annex of the mosque, where he could live for the time being.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-01978

From this point the account begins, in a characteristic way, to become a story of initiation. That is why, as far as possible, I shall let 'Ali ibn Fazel speak for himself. The shaykh who was the imam of this Shiite community—imam here in the purely liturgical sense, the person who leads the prayers—became his companion on the path of initiation. They spent every day together in long conversations. During his walks, however, 'Ali ibn Fazel noticed that there were no cultivated fields anywhere nearby.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-01979

Where, then, did the inhabitants obtain their food? He asked his companion this question, and it was surely the question that had to be asked. The shaykh answered: “Their provisions come from the Green Island in the White Sea, one of the islands belonging to the sons of the Imam who is lord of this age. — And how often each year,” I asked, “do these provisions arrive? — Twice a year. The first voyage has already taken place this year. We are still waiting for the second. — And how long,” I asked again, “before the next arrival? — Four months,” he told me.
